title: About & Full Data Explorer
text:
NFL Weekly Injury Reports (2010–2026): 88,730 weekly injury records from nflverse/nflverse-data, covering player names, teams, positions, primary injuries, and game statuses across 17 seasons.
NFL Playing Surface Analytics (elijah24/nfl-injuries): 105 detailed lower-extremity injury records (InjuryRecord.csv) and 267,005 play records (PlayList.csv) comparing Natural vs. Synthetic turf surfaces and injury severity (DM_M1 through DM_M42).
Multimodal Sports Injury Telemetry (anjalibhegam/multimodal-sports-injury-dataset): Biometric and biomechanical sensor readings including heart rate, ground reaction force (GRF), joint flexion angles, fatigue index, recovery score, and hydration level.
U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey (tidycensus): Live state-level population, median household income, and median age fetched via the Census API for each NFL team’s home state.

title: The Sideline Shift: When Concussions Stopped Being Playable
text:
While exploring the weekly NFL injury scatterplots on the Home tab, one pattern stands out sharply from every orthopedic injury in the dataset: a concussion listing today means something fundamentally different than it did twenty years ago. Using the same nflverse official weekly injury reports spanning full seasons from 2000 through 2025 (133,655 player-week records), the static chart below tracks the share of weekly injury-report appearances in which the player was officially ruled Out for that week’s game, comparing concussions against the four highest-volume physical injuries (knee, ankle, hamstring, and shoulder).









From 2000 through 2012, only 33.6% of weekly concussion listings resulted in a player sitting out that week’s game (597 of 1,776 appearances)—meaning roughly two out of every three players who landed on the report with a concussion still suited up on Sunday. Beginning in 2013, the NFL overhauled sideline oversight: introducing unaffiliated neurotrauma consultants on every sideline (2013), granting certified athletic trainer spotters in the stadium booth authority to call medical timeouts (2015), eliminating the “Probable” report designation while tightening return-to-play checkpoints (2016), and adding mandatory “no-go” ataxia criteria following high-profile prime-time head injuries (2022). Across the modern protocol era (2015–2025), 64.4% of concussion listings ended with the player ruled Out, peaking at 80.8% in 2019 and holding above 71% every season since 2022.
Comparing concussions against knee, ankle, hamstring, and shoulder injuries isolates medical policy from reporting mechanics. When the league retired the “Probable” tag in 2016, baseline Out rates rose modestly for orthopedic injuries too (from ~17% to ~35%), simply because minor bruises were no longer padded onto the denominator. Yet concussions vaulted nearly 30 percentage points above those structural joint and soft-tissue injuries. While helmet engineering, Guardian Caps, and playing-surface research aim to reduce biomechanical forces at the moment of impact, the clearest transformation in a quarter-century of NFL injury records came from governance after the whistle—turning a head injury from something players routinely taped over into an enforceable five-step medical gate.

    A["Impact Detected\n(Booth ATC Spotter / Sideline)"] --> B["Sideline Maddocks &\nVideo Review"]
    B --> C["Locker Room SCAT-6\n(Team MD + Unaffiliated Neuro)"]
    C --> D["Mandatory 5-Phase\nReturn-to-Participation Gate"]
    D --> E["71%–81% Ruled 'Out'\nfor Next Game (2022–2025)"]

Project Overview
This project combines 133,655 NFL injury records from 2000 through 2026 (nflverse-data and the NFL Playing Surface Analytics study) with multimodal athlete sensor telemetry and live annual U.S. Census Bureau (ACS) state demographics via tidycensus.
